blocks.body:
Euclid's argument shows that there are infinitely many primes, and small variations of it show that there are infinitely many primes of the form $4k+3$, or of the form $4k+1$. Arguments of that polynomial type are known to work only for special progressions, so they cannot answer the general question: if $\gcd(a,q)=1$, does the progression $a, a+q, a+2q, \dots$ contain infinitely many primes?

Dirichlet answered it in 1837. To each character $\chi$ modulo $q$ he attached a function $L(s,\chi)$, and he showed that the whole problem comes down to one fact: $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$ for every non-principal character $\chi$. This lesson builds these functions, explains why that fact is exactly what is needed, and proves it.

blocks.title: From Euler's proof to characters
blocks.body:
Start with Euler's proof that $\sum_p 1/p$ diverges, in the language of [[zeta]]. For real $s>1$ the Euler product gives
$$\log \zeta(s) = \sum_p -\log(1-p^{-s}) = \sum_p \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{1}{k p^{ks}}.$$
The terms with $k \ge 2$ add up to less than $\sum_p \sum_{k\ge 2} p^{-k} = \sum_p \frac{1}{p(p-1)} < 1$. Also $\zeta(s) = \frac{1}{s-1} + O(1)$ as $s \to 1^+$. Together,
$$\sum_p p^{-s} = \log\frac{1}{s-1} + O(1) \qquad (s \to 1^+),$$
which could not tend to infinity if there were only finitely many primes.

To run the same argument on a single residue class we need a way to pick out the integers $n \equiv a \pmod q$. Characters do this. By the orthogonality relations from [[dirichlet-characters]], if $\gcd(a,q)=1$ then
$$\frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\chi \bmod q} \overline{\chi}(a)\,\chi(n) = \begin{cases} 1 & n \equiv a \pmod q,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
Multiplying by $p^{-s}$ and summing over primes,
$$\sum_{p \equiv a \ (q)} p^{-s} = \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\chi} \overline{\chi}(a) \sum_p \chi(p)\, p^{-s}.$$
The principal character $\chi_0$ contributes $\sum_{p \nmid q} p^{-s} = \log\frac{1}{s-1} + O(1)$. So the theorem will follow once we know that, for every $\chi \ne \chi_0$, the sum $\sum_p \chi(p)p^{-s}$ stays bounded as $s \to 1^+$. That is a statement about $L(s,\chi)$.

blocks.title: Dirichlet L-function
blocks.body:
For a Dirichlet character $\chi$ modulo $q$ and $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$,
$$L(s,\chi) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\chi(n)}{n^s} = \prod_p \Bigl(1 - \frac{\chi(p)}{p^s}\Bigr)^{-1}.$$
The series converges absolutely because $|\chi(n)| \le 1$, and the product formula holds because $\chi$ is completely multiplicative (see [[dirichlet-series]]). The Euler product is what ties $L(s,\chi)$ to the values $\chi(p)$.

blocks.title: Three basic facts
blocks.body:
1. The principal character. Since $\chi_0(n)=1$ exactly when $\gcd(n,q)=1$, the Euler product gives $L(s,\chi_0) = \zeta(s)\prod_{p \mid q}(1-p^{-s})$. So $L(s,\chi_0)$ has a simple pole at $s=1$, just like $\zeta(s)$.

2. Non-principal characters converge further left. Let $A(x) = \sum_{n \le x}\chi(n)$. For $\chi \ne \chi_0$ the values of $\chi$ over any $q$ consecutive integers add up to $0$, and an incomplete block contains at most $\varphi(q)$ non-zero values, so $|A(x)| \le \varphi(q)$ for all $x$. By [[partial-summation]], if $f$ is positive and decreasing on $[t,u]$ then
$$\Bigl|\sum_{t < n \le u} \chi(n) f(n)\Bigr| = \Bigl|A(u)f(u) - A(t)f(t) - \int_t^u A(v) f'(v)\,dv\Bigr| \le 2\varphi(q) f(t).$$
With $f(n) = n^{-s}$ this shows that $\sum \chi(n)n^{-s}$ converges for every real $s>0$, with tails $|\sum_{n>t}\chi(n)n^{-s}| \le 2\varphi(q)t^{-s}$. In particular $L(1,\chi) = \sum_{n \ge 1}\chi(n)/n$ converges (not absolutely). The same argument applied to $\sum \chi(n)(\log n) n^{-s}$ shows that $L(s,\chi)$ is continuously differentiable for $s>0$.

3. A logarithm with a known main term. For $s>1$ put
$$\ell(s,\chi) = \sum_p \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{\chi(p)^k}{k\,p^{ks}}.$$
Using $-\log(1-z) = \sum_k z^k/k$ for $|z|<1$ in each Euler factor, $e^{\ell(s,\chi)} = L(s,\chi)$; in particular $L(s,\chi) \ne 0$ for $s>1$. As in Euler's computation, the terms with $k\ge 2$ contribute less than $1$ in absolute value, so
$$\ell(s,\chi) = \sum_p \chi(p)p^{-s} + O(1) \quad\text{uniformly for } s>1.$$

blocks.title: Dirichlet's theorem (conditional form)
blocks.body:
Let $q \ge 1$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$. If $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$ for every non-principal character $\chi$ modulo $q$, then
$$\sum_{p \equiv a \ (q)} \frac{1}{p^s} = \frac{1}{\varphi(q)}\log\frac{1}{s-1} + O(1) \qquad (s \to 1^+).$$
In particular, there are infinitely many primes $p \equiv a \pmod q$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Fix $\chi \ne \chi_0$. By fact 2, $L(s,\chi)$ is continuous on $[1,2]$; it is non-zero on $(1,2]$ by fact 3 and at $s=1$ by hypothesis. A continuous non-vanishing function on an interval has a continuous logarithm $\lambda(s)$ there, and $\lambda$ is bounded because $[1,2]$ is compact. On $(1,2]$ both $\lambda$ and $\ell(\cdot,\chi)$ are continuous logarithms of $L(\cdot,\chi)$, so their difference is a continuous function with values in $2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$, hence constant. Therefore $\ell(s,\chi)$ is bounded on $(1,2]$, and by fact 3 so is $\sum_p \chi(p)p^{-s}$.

For $\chi_0$ we have $\sum_p \chi_0(p)p^{-s} = \sum_p p^{-s} - \sum_{p \mid q}p^{-s} = \log\frac{1}{s-1} + O(1)$ by Euler's computation. Inserting both facts into the orthogonality formula of the first section gives the stated asymptotic. If there were only finitely many primes $p \equiv a \pmod q$, the left side would stay bounded as $s \to 1^+$, while the right side tends to infinity.

blocks.title: The finer statement
blocks.body:
With Mertens-type estimates in place of the limit $s \to 1^+$, the same strategy gives the key statement: for $\gcd(a,q)=1$,
$$\sum_{\substack{p \le x \\ p \equiv a \ (q)}} \frac{1}{p} = \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \log\log x + O(1),$$
where the $O(1)$ depends on $q$. Compared with $\sum_{p \le x} 1/p = \log\log x + O(1)$ from [[mertens]], each of the $\varphi(q)$ admissible classes receives an equal share. The extra input is that $\sum_{p \le x}\chi(p)/p$ stays bounded for $\chi \ne \chi_0$, again a consequence of $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$; we omit it (Apostol, Chapter 7, proves the version with weights $\log p/p$).

The stronger statement that each class contains asymptotically $\pi(x)/\varphi(q)$ primes up to $x$ is the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions (de la Vallée Poussin, 1896). It needs $L(s,\chi) \ne 0$ on the whole line $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$; see [[pnt]] and [[zero-free-region]].

blocks.title: Why L(1, χ) is not zero: complex characters
blocks.body:
Everything now rests on $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$. The first step is a positivity property of the product of all the $L$-functions modulo $q$.

Lemma. For real $s>1$, $\prod_{\chi \bmod q} L(s,\chi)$ is real and at least $1$.

Proof. Summing the series for $\ell(s,\chi)$ over all $\chi$ and using orthogonality,
$$\sum_{\chi}\ell(s,\chi) = \sum_p\sum_{k\ge 1}\frac{1}{k p^{ks}}\sum_\chi \chi(p^k) = \varphi(q)\sum_{p^k \equiv 1 \ (q)} \frac{1}{k p^{ks}} \ \ge\ 0.$$
Exponentiating gives $\prod_\chi L(s,\chi) = e^{\sum_\chi \ell(s,\chi)} \ge 1$.

Now suppose $\chi \ne \overline{\chi}$ (a complex character) and $L(1,\chi)=0$. Then also $L(1,\overline\chi) = \overline{L(1,\chi)} = 0$. As $s \to 1^+$: the factor $L(s,\chi_0)$ is at most $C/(s-1)$; the two factors $L(s,\chi)$ and $L(s,\overline\chi)$ are each at most $C(s-1)$ in absolute value, because they are differentiable at $1$ and vanish there; every other factor is bounded. So the product is $O(s-1)$ and tends to $0$, contradicting the lemma. Hence $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$ for every complex character.

For a real character $\chi = \overline\chi$ this argument gives nothing: a single zero at $s=1$ would exactly cancel the simple pole of $L(s,\chi_0)$, and the product could still be at least $1$. Real characters need their own argument.

blocks.title: Non-vanishing for real characters
blocks.body: If $\chi$ is a real non-principal character modulo $q$, then $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $r(n) = \sum_{d \mid n}\chi(d)$. This is multiplicative, and on prime powers $r(p^k) = 1 + \chi(p) + \dots + \chi(p)^k$ equals $k+1$, $1$, or ($1$ if $k$ is even, $0$ if $k$ is odd) according as $\chi(p) = 1, 0, -1$. Hence $r(n) \ge 0$ for all $n$, and $r(n) \ge 1$ when $n$ is a perfect square.

Consider $G(x) = \sum_{n \le x} r(n)/\sqrt n$. Keeping only the squares $n = m^2$,
$$G(x) \ \ge\ \sum_{m \le \sqrt x}\frac{1}{m} \ \ge\ \log\sqrt x = \tfrac12\log x.$$
On the other hand $G(x) = \sum_{dm \le x}\chi(d)/\sqrt{dm}$. Put $y = \sqrt x$ and split the pairs $(d,m)$ with $dm \le x$ into those with $d \le y$ and those with $d > y$ (which forces $m < y$):
$$G(x) = \sum_{d \le y}\frac{\chi(d)}{\sqrt d}\sum_{m \le x/d}\frac{1}{\sqrt m} \;+\; \sum_{m \le y}\frac{1}{\sqrt m}\sum_{y < d \le x/m}\frac{\chi(d)}{\sqrt d}.$$
We use two estimates, with constants depending only on $q$: comparison with an integral gives $\sum_{m \le t} m^{-1/2} = 2\sqrt t + c_0 + O(t^{-1/2})$ for $t \ge 1$ and some constant $c_0$; and fact 2 gives $|\sum_{t<d\le u}\chi(d)d^{-1/2}| \le 2\varphi(q)t^{-1/2}$ and $\sum_{d \le y}\chi(d)/d = L(1,\chi) + O(1/y)$.

In the first double sum, the inner sum is $2\sqrt{x/d} + c_0 + O(\sqrt{d/x})$, so the first part equals
$$2\sqrt x\sum_{d\le y}\frac{\chi(d)}{d} + c_0\sum_{d\le y}\frac{\chi(d)}{\sqrt d} + O\Bigl(\frac{y}{\sqrt x}\Bigr) = 2\sqrt x\,L(1,\chi) + O(1),$$
because $\sqrt x \cdot O(1/y) = O(1)$, the partial sums of the convergent series $\sum \chi(d)/\sqrt d$ are bounded, and $y/\sqrt x = 1$. In the second part each inner sum is $O(y^{-1/2})$ and $\sum_{m \le y} m^{-1/2} \le 2\sqrt y$, so it is $O(1)$. Therefore
$$G(x) = 2\sqrt x\,L(1,\chi) + O(1).$$
If $L(1,\chi)$ were $0$, $G(x)$ would be bounded, contradicting $G(x) \ge \frac12\log x$.

blocks.title: The two classes modulo 4
blocks.body: Let $\chi_4$ be the non-principal character modulo $4$ ($\chi_4(n) = 1, -1, 0$ for $n \equiv 1, 3$, even). Compute $L(1,\chi_4)$, explain how the proof separates the primes $p \equiv 1$ from $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and compare the sums $\sum 1/p$ over the two classes for $p \le 10^6$.
blocks.solution:
Here $L(1,\chi_4) = 1 - \frac13 + \frac15 - \frac17 + \dots = \frac{\pi}{4}$ (Leibniz's series, the value of $\arctan 1$). The two indicator functions are $\frac12(\chi_0 + \chi_4)$ for the class $1$ and $\frac12(\chi_0 - \chi_4)$ for the class $3$, so
$$\sum_{p \equiv 1\,(4)} p^{-s} = \tfrac12\Bigl(\sum_{p>2}p^{-s} + \sum_p\chi_4(p)p^{-s}\Bigr),\qquad \sum_{p \equiv 3\,(4)} p^{-s} = \tfrac12\Bigl(\sum_{p>2}p^{-s} - \sum_p\chi_4(p)p^{-s}\Bigr).$$
The first sum in each bracket is $\log\frac{1}{s-1} + O(1)$, and the second stays bounded because $L(1,\chi_4) = \pi/4 \ne 0$. So both classes get half of the divergence.

Numerically, for $p \le 10^6$ one finds $\sum_{p\equiv 1\,(4)} 1/p \approx 1.026$ and $\sum_{p \equiv 3\,(4)}1/p \approx 1.361$, while $\frac12\log\log 10^6 \approx 1.313$. Both sums grow like $\frac12\log\log x$; their difference is a bounded quantity (the prime $3$ alone contributes $1/3$ to it).

blocks.title: Lattice points and the value π/4
blocks.body: For $\chi = \chi_4$ the function $r(n) = \sum_{d\mid n}\chi_4(d)$ from the proof has a geometric meaning: the number of pairs $(u,v)\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ with $u^2+v^2 = n$ equals $4r(n)$ for $n \ge 1$ (Jacobi's two-square formula, see [[sums-of-squares]]). Use this to show again that $L(1,\chi_4) = \pi/4$.
blocks.solution:
Summing over $n \le x$, the left side counts lattice points $(u,v) \ne (0,0)$ in the disc $u^2+v^2 \le x$, which is $\pi x + O(\sqrt x)$ (compare each lattice point with the unit square it is the corner of). So $\sum_{n\le x}r(n) = \frac{\pi}{4}x + O(\sqrt x)$.

On the other hand $\sum_{n \le x}r(n) = \sum_{dm \le x}\chi_4(d)$. Splitting at $y = \sqrt x$ as in the proof (Dirichlet's hyperbola method),
$$\sum_{dm\le x}\chi_4(d) = \sum_{d\le y}\chi_4(d)\Bigl\lfloor\frac{x}{d}\Bigr\rfloor + \sum_{m \le y}A\Bigl(\frac{x}{m}\Bigr) - A(y)\lfloor y\rfloor,$$
with $A(t) = \sum_{n\le t}\chi_4(n) \in \{0,1\}$. The first sum is $x\sum_{d \le y}\chi_4(d)/d + O(y) = x\,L(1,\chi_4) + O(\sqrt x)$, and the other two terms are $O(\sqrt x)$. Comparing, $x\,L(1,\chi_4) = \frac{\pi}{4}x + O(\sqrt x)$; divide by $x$ and let $x \to \infty$.

For $x = 10^6$ the disc contains $3\,141\,549$ lattice points, so $\sum_{n \le 10^6} r(n) = 785\,387$, against $\frac{\pi}{4}\cdot 10^6 \approx 785\,398$. The sum $G(x)$ of the proof behaves as predicted too: at $x = 10^6$, $G(x) - 2\sqrt x\cdot\frac{\pi}{4} \approx -0.99$.

blocks.title: Two progressions without L-functions
blocks.body: Prove, with elementary arguments only, that there are infinitely many primes $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ and infinitely many primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
blocks.solution:
Class $3$. Given any finite list $p_1,\dots,p_k$ of primes $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, let $N = 4p_1\cdots p_k - 1$. Then $N$ is odd and $N \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. A product of integers that are all $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ is $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, so $N$ has a prime factor $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. It is not any $p_i$, since $N \equiv -1 \pmod{p_i}$.

Class $1$. Given any finite list $p_1,\dots,p_k$ of primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, let $M = (2p_1\cdots p_k)^2 + 1$ and let $p$ be a prime factor of $M$. Then $p$ is odd, $p \ne p_i$, and $(2p_1\cdots p_k)^2 \equiv -1 \pmod p$, so $-1$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$. By [[quadratic-residues]] this forces $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

Both proofs use a polynomial whose prime divisors are confined to the desired classes; as the introduction says, this trick does not extend to general progressions.

blocks.body:
- The Euler product does not converge absolutely at $s=1$, and its convergence there is not evident (it is in fact a deep fact, of the strength of the prime number theorem for progressions). So $L(1,\chi)$ is defined as the sum of the conditionally convergent series $\sum \chi(n)/n$, equivalently the limit of $L(s,\chi)$ as $s \to 1^+$, not by putting $s=1$ into the product.
- The condition $\gcd(a,q)=1$ is essential: if $\gcd(a,q) = d > 1$, every term of the progression is divisible by $d$, so it contains at most one prime.
- If $\chi$ is induced by a primitive character $\chi^*$, then $L(s,\chi) = L(s,\chi^*)\prod_{p\mid q}(1-\chi^*(p)p^{-s})$. The extra factors do not vanish at $s=1$, so non-vanishing at $1$ can be checked on primitive characters.

For real characters Dirichlet went further and computed $L(1,\chi)$ exactly in terms of class numbers of quadratic forms: see [[class-number-formula]]. How small $L(1,\chi)$ can be, and how close to $1$ a real zero of $L(s,\chi)$ can lie, is the subject of [[siegel-zeros]] and [[no-siegel]]; the generalized Riemann hypothesis [[grh]] asserts that all non-trivial zeros lie on $\operatorname{Re} s = \frac12$. The zeros control the error term for primes in progressions through the [[explicit-formula]], and averages of $|L(\frac12 + it,\chi)|^2$ are the subject of [[moments]].

The template generalizes: [[hecke-l]] attaches $L$-functions to characters of ideal class groups of number fields, and the conjecture of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer [[bsd]] predicts the behaviour at $s=1$ of the $L$-function of an elliptic curve.

1. Using the primitive root $2$ modulo $5$, list the four characters modulo $5$ and write the indicator function of the class $n \equiv 2 \pmod 5$ as a combination of them.
2. Prove that $|\sum_{n\le x}\chi(n)| \le \varphi(q)$ for every non-principal $\chi$ modulo $q$, and deduce that $\sum_n \chi(n)/n$ converges.
3. For the real character $\chi$ modulo $3$, compute $r(n) = \sum_{d\mid n}\chi(d)$ for $1 \le n \le 12$ and check that $r(n) \ge 0$, with $r(n) \ge 1$ at the squares.
